title: The sisters' songs, five

segments.voice: Yesterday, Subha asked a man what is an eye, and her refusal held. Today, the last of the sisters, and a refusal of a different size.
screen: `WHAT IS AN EYE.` → `A REFUSAL OF A DIFFERENT SIZE.`

segments.voice: A palace. A wedding date set. The groom is a king named Anikaratta, and he's already on his way. The bride, Princess Sumedha, has told her parents again and again that she doesn't want this life. She wants to go forth, to become a nun. They've pleaded. They've reminded her what she'd give up. And now, the poem says, she takes her own hair and cuts it off, shuts the door, and sits down to meditate while the king's procession comes up the road.
screen: `A WEDDING DATE. A KING ON THE ROAD.` → `SHE WANTS TO GO FORTH.` → `SHE CUTS OFF HER HAIR.`

segments.voice: Here's what's easy to miss. Sumedha doesn't sneak out a window. Her song is long because most of it is her talking, to her mother, to her father, and finally to the king himself. In paraphrase: this body is fragile; pleasures promise more than they give; a crown won't stop old age; I want what doesn't fall apart. She lays it out image after image, and she keeps calling them by tender names. Then Anikaratta walks in, ready for a wedding, and finds a woman with cropped hair who answers him with the same calm. The poem says he listened. He agreed. Her parents let her go, and she went forth and found the freedom she'd been describing. Notice the shape of her choice. She didn't wait until it was easy. She didn't win by force or by running. She chose, said why, stayed kind, and kept choosing until the people who loved her could hear it. That's the close of the sisters: Mutta's mortar, Patacara's lamp, Ambapali's mirror, Subha's eye, and Sumedha's hair on the floor.
screen: `NOT OUT A WINDOW.` · `A CROWN WON'T STOP OLD AGE.` · `THE KING LISTENED.` · `CHOSE, SAID WHY, STAYED KIND.` · then, large: `SHE CHOSE.`

segments.voice: Sit up tall, feet flat, hands open on your knees, a posture that's steady without being stiff. Bring one choice you've made that you mean to keep. Hold it there in the body, calm and upright, the whole sit.
The sisters' songs, ending with Sumedha's: a princess who chose to go forth and talked her family and her groom into letting her.
Your line: she chose. And she stayed gentle the whole time she was choosing. Five sisters, heard.

howItsDone: Sumedha's song closes the Therigatha; in Buddhist communities, going forth as a monk or nun customarily involves shaving the head, and asking the family's permission is part of the tradition's ordination rules.
